newsitem.title: UK: EMI sidesteps market concerns about euro FX policy.
newsitem.headline: EMI sidesteps market concerns about euro FX policy.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute (EMI) report on monetary instruments to be used by the future European central bank (ECB) sidesteps key currency market concerns about exchange rate policy after monetary union, analysts said.
The big issue for traders is who sets policy direction not the policy tools themselves, said analysts. The detail outlined in Friday's report was welcome but unsurprising, they said.
"Today's report was very much an operational document and, as such, there was nothing in it markets could fault," said Avinash Persaud, currency research head at JP Morgan in Europe.

"The forex market is looking to see who sets the objectives of exchange rate policy because of growing concern it will be subject to a large degree of guidance from the European council," said Persaud.
Traders believe the European council of member states goverments would invest a greater degree of political influence on the exchange rate than the central bank may want.

The EMI said it ruled out the use of exchange rate targeting with currencies outside the euro area on the grounds that it may interfere with the central bank's main priority of price stability. Instead, it said it favoured money supply or inflation targets.

The report said the high level of intra-European Union (EU) trade meant exchange rate developments would "most likely constitute less of a concern for the conduct of monetary policy than is currently the case for many NCBs," or national central banks.

Nevertheless, a perceived desire among many European governments, most vocally from France, to prevent excessive strength of the new euro against the dollar leaves many market analysts sceptical that the exchange rate will not be subject to some manipulation.

In an interview with Le Figaro in December, former French president Valery Giscard d"Estaing urged the establishment of a special parliamentary committee to supervise the planned euro currency and balance the power of a European central bank.

The debate on relative euro/dollar levels was triggered in France in the final months of 1996, led partly by calls from Giscard for a weaker franc against what he viewed as a chronically undervalued dollar to help boost employment.
Many parliament members and even two Bank of France council members supported Giscard's views.
Analysts pointed out that like most countries in Europe at present, the exchange regime is directed by government Treasuries and the central banks operate within that framework.

"The Maastricht Treaty already provides good guidelines on how exchange rate policy must be formulated," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch in London. "The ECB must act within the general council's general guidelines as long as price stability is not undermined."

Article 109.2 of the Maastricht Treaty states "In the absence of an exchange rate system in relation to one or more of non-EC currencies...the council...may formulate general orientations for exchange rate policy in relation to these currencies (non-EC)."

Neil MacKinnon, chief economist at Citibank, said "It's hard to believe the exchange rate will have no influence on policy given the desire in Europe not to have an overvalued euro and given that the G-3 will almost certainly have an interest in reducing currency volatility between the euro, dollar and yen."
